skill.description: Adds Caffeine AI authorization guidance for role-based access control, Internet Identity login, user profiles, and verified email handling.

security_audit.summary: Static findings are false positives caused by Markdown links, inline code, and fenced examples. No shell execution, arbitrary filesystem access, network exfiltration, reconnaissance, or prompt injection was found. The remaining concern is the documented first-user admin bootstrap behavior.

remediation.issue: First authenticated user automatically becomes admin without a token or secret.
remediation.suggestion: Require an explicit owner principal, deployment-time admin claim token, or private setup step before public access is enabled.

remediation.issue: Documentation does not warn about public exposure before the first admin signs in.
remediation.suggestion: Add a clear warning and setup checklist for claiming admin ownership before sharing the application URL.

semantic_findings.title: First Authenticated User Becomes Admin
semantic_findings.description: The skill states that the first authenticated user automatically becomes admin without a token or secret. A public deployment could let an unintended user claim administrator access before the owner signs in.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The behavior is explicitly documented twice. The impact depends on deployment controls, but the ownership claim risk is clear.

content.user_title: Add Role-Based Authorization to Caffeine Apps
content.value_statement: Access rules are hard to apply consistently across backend and frontend code. This skill provides Caffeine AI patterns for roles, login state, profiles, and verified email.
actual_capabilities: Shows how to include MixinAuthorization in a Motoko backend.
Defines admin, user, and guest role patterns for public methods.
Provides profile API examples tied to the caller principal.
Explains verified email capture through Internet Identity attributes.
Guides frontend login, logout, cache clearing, and auth state checks.
Includes a migration checklist for the v1 authorization package.
limitations: It is documentation and examples, not a standalone authorization service.
It assumes Caffeine AI, Motoko, and Internet Identity packages are available.
The first authenticated user becomes admin unless the app adds stronger setup controls.
Custom authentication requires removing the provided authorization package.

use_cases.title: Protect Personal Data
use_cases.description: Add caller-based profile access so users can view and update only their own records.

use_cases.title: Add Admin Workflows
use_cases.description: Use role checks to restrict sensitive operations to administrators.

use_cases.title: Wire Login UI
use_cases.description: Connect Internet Identity state to login screens, logout behavior, and cached data cleanup.

prompt_templates.title: Add Basic Authorization
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new Caffeine AI app.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use extension-authorization to add role-based authorization to my Caffeine AI app. Include the backend imports, access control state, and required mixin placement.

prompt_templates.title: Protect User Profiles
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate profile access for personal data.
prompt_templates.prompt: Use extension-authorization to add profile methods for the current caller. Make sure users can read their own profile and admins can review other profiles.

prompt_templates.title: Add Verified Email Handling
prompt_templates.prompt: Use extension-authorization to store verified Internet Identity email attributes after sign-in. Add a safe getter for the current caller.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Authorization Coverage
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced review of existing app access rules.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Caffeine AI backend with extension-authorization. Identify public methods that need admin, user, or ownership guards, then propose precise changes.

output_examples.input: A new Caffeine AI app needs authorization before storing user profiles.
output_examples.output: The response adds the authorization mixin, initializes access control state, and describes caller-based profile methods with role checks.

output_examples.input: An app needs a login button that works after page reloads.
output_examples.output: The response explains the correct auth state fields, disabled button states, logout cache clearing, and authenticated screen gating.

output_examples.input: A team wants to migrate to the v1 authorization package.
output_examples.output: The response lists package version updates, the new mixin argument, frontend dependency requirements, and verification steps.

best_practices: Place MixinAuthorization in main.mo and pass accessControlState to dependent mixins.
Guard every sensitive public method with admin, user, or ownership checks.
Clear cached application data whenever the user logs out.
anti_patterns: Do not rely on isLoginSuccess to decide whether restored sessions are authenticated.
Do not expose application data before the user is authenticated.
Do not leave the authorization package installed while omitting the required mixin.

faq.question: What does this skill help build?
faq.answer: It helps add role-based authorization, Internet Identity login handling, profile access, and verified email handling to Caffeine AI apps.

faq.question: Does it create a full authentication provider?
faq.answer: No. It uses Caffeine AI and Internet Identity packages and shows how to integrate them safely.

faq.question: Which roles are described?
faq.answer: The examples describe admin, user, and guest roles with guard patterns for public backend methods.

faq.question: Can it store verified email addresses?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows how to capture verified Internet Identity attributes through the authorization mixin callback.

faq.question: What should happen on logout?
faq.answer: The frontend should clear authentication state and cached application data so another user cannot see stale information.

faq.question: What is the main security caveat?
faq.answer: The first authenticated user becomes admin, so deployments need a controlled ownership setup before public access.
